newsitem.title: UK: Softer UK PMI, money data point to steady rates.
newsitem.headline: Softer UK PMI, money data point to steady rates.

text.p: Slower growth in Britain's purchasing managers' index (PMI) and a slight slowing in money supply in February will calm any immediate fears that interest rates may head up in the immediate future.
But analysts said the data, while showing the expected dampening effect of sterling strength on inflation, were not benign enough to eliminate the need for tighter monetary policy later this year.
"It was generally a pretty good PMI survey," said Mark Miller, UK economist at Morgan Stanley in London.
"We have the underlying recovery in manufacturing balanced against fairly benign price pressures."
The PMI index fell to 53.5 in February from 53.9 in January, a level which still showed expansion in manufacturing. The prices index showed the largest drop since July last year.
Provisional M0 money supply grew by 6.5 percent in the year to February, down from 7.3 percent growth in January.
"The price data mean interest rates are obviously going to remain steady for the near term," said Stephen Hannah, head of research at IBJ International in London.
He said the numbers gave a similar picture of Britain's economy to that in the U.S., where relatively strong growth has so far not resulted in the pick-up in inflation many had feared.

Economists noted that the consumer sector, which has sparked inflationary worries in recent months with healthy performances in retail and consumer prices, remained robust -- despite a softer consumer credit figure for January.
Net consumer credit rose 853 million sterling in January versus a 983 million rise in December, but analysts said the overall trend was intact.

"The consumer story is still in place," said Miller. "Although the consumer credit figure fell back slightly, we still have a 12-month growth rate of 16.7 percent which is running at around six-year highs."

But with only moderate growth in the manufacturing sector and signs in Monday's PMI survey that price pressures are starting to recede, financial markets would be relatively happy to see monetary policy holding steady for now, analysts said.

Miller said the case for the rate rise was still there, but it could be pushed forward to the second half of 1997, while IBJ's Hannah said it was little more than a case of tweaking policy to keep inflation in check.

"The size of the rate increase we need is not of a draconian nature," said Hannah, adding that 50 to 100 basis points should be enough to bring inflation down to the government's 2.5 percent rolling target.

Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke, who was due to give a speech to the British Retail Consortium later on Monday, is expected to signal that rates will stay on hold until the election, due by May 22 at the latest.
Monday's Financial Times said Clarke will point to the braking influence on inflation of sterling's dramatic rally since the summer of last year.
Analysts said the PMI and money supply data would provide welcome ammunition for the Chancellor in his bid to keep rates at 6.0 percent.

While the survey showed the recovery in the manufacturing sector was still in place, Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets said several other factors meant this pick-up was unlikely to prompt inflation concerns.

The employment index, which slowed to 51.2 in February from 53.1 in January, was now "dangerously close to signalling a new bout of job-shedding in industry", Loynes said, and the worst of the impact of sterling was still to be felt in manufacturing.
